title: Trapped-ion quantum simulation of (1+1)D SU(2) lattice gauge theory via loop-string-hadron formulation
authors: Toshiaki Kaji, Jesse R. Stryker, Yutaro Iiyama, Lento Nagano, Enrico Rinaldi, Christian W. Bauer, Koji Terashi
abstract: We present a quantum simulation of the SU(2) lattice gauge theory in 1+1 dimensions with one flavor of fermions, performed using the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H2. This work is based on the loop-string-hadron (LSH) formulation of the gauge theory, and is distinguished by using qubits to represent both bosonic-gauge and fermionic-matter degrees of freedom. Furthermore, we access the $j=1$ electric-flux sector beyond the $j_{\max}=1/2$ truncation commonly used in SU(2) quantum simulations. To that end, we digitize an electric-field degree of freedom using a multiqubit register for representing the bosonic quantum number. Our simulation therefore synthesizes several key ingredients relevant to quantum simulations in higher spatial dimensions, in particular explicit local gauge-field degrees of freedom represented here by a multiqubit bosonic register, while relying solely on circuit-construction optimizations that are expected to scale polynomially with lattice size. This work demonstrates that modern quantum hardware is increasingly able to accommodate the features of complicated but physically important lattice gauge theories while successfully reproducing the expected Trotterized dynamics.
summary: This work presents a quantum simulation of the SU(2) lattice gauge theory using trapped ions, employing the advanced loop-string-hadron formulation. By mapping the theory onto qubits, the authors simulate the time evolution of the electric field, demonstrating that current quantum hardware can tackle complex gauge theories while achieving substantial noise reduction through sophisticated error mitigation protocols.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating interacting quantum field theories, specifically SU(2) lattice gauge theory, without relying on perturbative methods or encountering the sign problem.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated that modern trapped-ion quantum hardware can simulate complex lattice gauge theories, achieving significant error reduction through advanced error mitigation techniques.
method: The simulation uses the loop-string-hadron (LSH) formulation to map the gauge theory Hamiltonian onto qubit operators, followed by Trotterized real-time quantum evolution.
model_or_system: The system is an SU(2) lattice gauge theory in 1+1 dimensions with one flavor of fermions. The simulation is implemented on the trapped-ion Quantinuum System Model H2, utilizing qubits to encode both bosonic gauge and fermionic matter degrees of freedom.
key_observables: Time evolution of the electric-field energy density across the lattice.
important_parameters: The simulation accesses the $j=1$ electric-flux sector, surpassing the typical $j_{	ext{max}}=1/2$ truncation, and uses a minimal four-site lattice.
main_assumptions: The simulation relies on the LSH formulation to manage Gauss's law constraints and employs error mitigation techniques like rescaling and post-selection to combat hardware noise.
figures_summary: Figure 12 compares the calculated electric energy density over time, contrasting theoretical predictions with results obtained from a quantum emulator using raw, depolarizing error-mitigated, and post-selection error-mitigated measurements.
paper_structure: The paper reviews the LSH setup, details the circuit construction and necessary optimizations, discusses the application of error mitigation techniques, and finally presents the simulation results using data from the H2-2 platform.
why_interesting: The direct use of trapped ions to simulate a complex, non-Abelian lattice gauge theory is highly relevant, showcasing the capability of trapped-ion platforms to handle intricate, constrained many-body dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The lattice and its degrees of freedom. (a) A de- piction of the lattice with four staggered sites, open bound- ary conditions, and a single unit of external flux sourced at the right-side boundary. (b) A depiction of the LSH de- grees of freedom relevant to the system. Each box corre- sponds to one qubit used to represent the indicated quantum numbers. (c) A cartoon illustration of the LSH basis state |(0, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1), (0, 0, 2), (1, 0, 1)⟩, with a certain set of spec- ified boundary flux values. Red dots are drawn to illustrate the Abelian Gauss’s law: the units of gauge flux at either end of a link must be balanced.

FIG. 2. First-order Trotterized circuit for 4 lattice sites. Each labeled block represents the propagator associated with the indicated Hamiltonian subterm rather than an elementary gate. Blocks spanning multiple register lines indicate the qubits on which the corresponding subterm acts; they do not necessarily imply entangling operations between all of those qubits.

FIG. 3. An example of error conversion in the hopping subterm H(j=1) I (r = 0). Registers i(r), o(r), ℓ(r) are assigned for ni(r), no(r), nℓ(r), respectively. The gray box represents the diagonal block, implemented using RZ and CX gates. (a) The original circuit without the error insertion. (b) A Z-error between H gates is converted into the X error, which is further propagated and spreads out. (c) A Z-error outside two H gates propagates and can change some angles, but is not converted to X-errors, at least in this subcircuit.

FIG. 4. Estimated effective depolarizing-noise parameters ob- tained using the test circuits. The red squares, yellow trian- gles, and green inverted triangles correspond to the observ- ables on links 0, 1, and 2, respectively.

FIG. 5. Discard rate and number of shots remaining after post-selection as functions of the number of Trotter steps. The black left vertical axis corresponds to the discard rate shown by black circles, while the red right vertical axis cor- responds to the number of remaining shots shown by red di- amonds.
